state.case_summary:
A 40-year-old man presented with 1 week of difficulty voiding and was catheterized for urinary retention. Ultrasonography revealed a large prostatic mass, and his prostate-specific antigen level was 0.62 ng/mL (normal <4.0). He denied pain, fever, or abdominal distension. Physical examination was unremarkable, and complete blood count, routine chemistries, and tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA-125, SCC antigen, CYFRA) were all within normal limits. Digital rectal examination revealed an enlarged prostate with palpable nodules and an ill-defined border. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed a heterogeneous prostatic mass. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 5.5-cm heterogeneous lesion in the right prostate lobe, and cystoscopy raised suspicion for bladder invasion. Positron emission tomography–CT and colonoscopy suggested rectal invasion. A provisional diagnosis of prostatic sarcoma was made, and a transrectal needle biopsy was performed. The biopsy result was interpreted as either prostatic stromal sarcoma or prostatic stromal tumor of uncertain malignant potential.
